title: Solomon and the Temple
hook: David stood at the window and saw beauty—but he sent others to bring it, others to conceal it, others to die for it, while he himself remained behind, safe in the city where kings were not supposed to be. That single verb—*to send*—becomes the architecture of his downfall, stretched like a shadow across chapter after chapter until Nathan the prophet arrives with a story about a rich man who took what wasn't his. The same king who would not go to war in person would later be forbidden from building the house of God, his hands too stained for such sacred work—yet his son Solomon, born of the very union that began in sin, would raise that temple and fill it with the glory of divine presence. Here is the terrible, redemptive paradox woven through these chapters: God's covenant moves forward not because of our worthiness but in spite of our fractures, and the throne built for justice must first be occupied by men who have learned what it means to be judged.
